name: Harry Stafford
bio: New Jersey farm boy and, from 1876, the companion of Whitman's Camden years. He was eighteen and working as an errand boy at the Camden New Republic when Whitman, fifty-seven and still recovering from the stroke of 1873, came in to work on the Centennial Leaves of Grass. His parents George and Susan Stafford were tenant farmers at White Horse Farm near Kirkwood, and it was there, beside Timber Creek, that Whitman took the sun-and-mud cures he wrote up in Specimen Days. The two shared a top-floor bedroom at the farm; travelling, Whitman called him 'my nephew' and insisted on a shared bed. Whitman gave him a friendship ring, which Stafford returned more than once in the course of a quarrelsome attachment. He drifted between jobs, went back to the farm, and married Eva Westcott - in 1883 by the Whitman Archive's note on the letters, in 1884 by Kantrowitz's reference entry, a conflict left standing. Whitman left him the silver watch he had originally meant for Peter Doyle.
